strengths: The conditional-kernel construction is a useful and reasonably original extension of Clifford-steerable CNNs. Conditioning an equivariant implicit kernel on equivariantly pooled input features provides global context with little stated computational overhead.

The manuscript clearly motivates the missing angular-frequency components in the original CSCNN construction and gives an intuitive O(2) algebraic example of how additional multivectors can generate frequency-2 terms.

The paper evaluates several PDE families, including Euclidean and relativistic settings, and consistently reports improvements over the original CSCNN. The inclusion of data-scaling curves and a numerical equivariance check is directionally valuable.

Presentation is generally clear and visually polished, with helpful diagrams and a logical progression from steerable convolutions to the proposed conditional construction. The work poses no evident human-subject, privacy, or dual-use concern; its main ethical consideration is computational cost, for which the hardware and approximate model sizes are at least partially reported.
weaknesses: The central completeness claim is unsupported. Section 4.4 explicitly states completeness only as Conjecture 4.1. The algebraic examples establish that some previously missing frequency-2 terms can occur for suitable auxiliary multivectors, not that the entire kernel basis is complete for arbitrary O(p,q), feature types, conditioning values, or network depths. Predictive benchmark performance cannot validate mathematical completeness. This directly conflicts with the title and repeated claims that the method provides a complete basis.

The implemented pooling appears not to satisfy the symmetries claimed by the theory. Proposition 4.1 requires a translation-invariant and O(p,q)-equivariant conditioning operator. Appendix B instead pools through a fixed centered circular/spherical mask. Such a mask is not translation invariant under general translations, and a Euclidean ball is not invariant under Lorentz transformations O(1,2). Consequently, the implemented model is not shown to be E(p,q)-equivariant, especially on the relativistic Maxwell task. The paper tests only an under-specified E(2) case and provides no Lorentz-equivariance measurement.

The continuum treatment of global mean pooling is incomplete: a normalized global mean is not generally defined on L2(R^{p,q}) over an infinite noncompact domain, while pooling over a finite window introduces boundary assumptions that affect translation equivariance. Periodic boundaries or another precise domain/action convention are needed.

The empirical gains do not isolate the proposed explanation. Conditioning turns a linear convolution into an input-adaptive nonlinear operator with global context, so improvements over CSCNN could arise from generic dynamic filtering rather than recovery of missing basis components. Essential ablations are absent, including scalar-only or invariant conditioning, alternative pooling, shuffled/constant conditions, matched non-equivariant dynamic kernels, and direct approximation of known analytical steerable kernels.

The evaluation is insufficiently reproducible. Most headline results appear only as plots without numerical values, variances, numbers of seeds, or confidence intervals. Exact learning rates, batch sizes, training steps, stopping rules, initialization, augmentation, and baseline-tuning procedures are not reported; “trained to convergence” is not a reproducible protocol. No code or artifact availability statement is provided.

Baseline fairness is difficult to assess. Some baselines are rerun while others are imported from earlier papers; SWE-5 compares substantially different parameter counts and potentially different training protocols. Runtime, memory, and throughput are not measured, despite efficiency being part of the motivation.

The equivariance experiment is too under-specified to substantiate exact equivariance: it omits the transformation distribution, number of samples, interpolation procedure, boundary handling, and dispersion of errors. Its nonstandard relative-error denominator can also become unstable. Arbitrary rotations on finite grids and translations interacting with the fixed mask are not investigated.

The proof appendix contains imprecisions, including the tautological Eq. 33 and an unjustified claim that equality of kernel-network outputs holds if and only if the conditioning inputs agree; that implication would require injectivity. Although the stated sufficiency direction may be repairable, the current presentation weakens confidence in the theoretical treatment.

Limitations are only partially acknowledged. The authors identify the unproved conjecture and restrictive mean-field conditioning as future work, but do not acknowledge that their finite masking can violate translation and pseudo-orthogonal equivariance or that benchmark accuracy does not demonstrate basis completeness. These are central limitations rather than merely reduced scope.

strengths: Soundness: The derivation of an equivariance condition for input-conditioned convolutions is a sensible contribution, and the proposed construction—conditioning an implicit Clifford-steerable kernel on an equivariantly pooled feature—is plausible. The measured equivariance errors are close to those of the original layer (3.4e-7 versus 2.4e-7).

Significance: Improving the expressivity of Clifford-steerable CNNs could be useful for symmetry-aware PDE forecasting, including pseudo-Euclidean settings that many standard equivariant architectures cannot handle.

Presentation: The paper has a generally coherent progression from the limitation of CSCNNs to the conditional construction, efficient implementation, and PDE experiments. It also openly labels its general completeness statement as a conjecture rather than presenting it as a proved theorem.

Originality: Applying equivariant input-dependent kernel generation to CSCNNs is a meaningful, if incremental, extension. The reported improvements over the matched CSCNN baseline across several PDE settings are promising.
weaknesses: The central claim is unsupported. The title promises a “complete kernel basis,” but Section 4.4 states completeness only as Conjecture 4.1. The analysis merely shows that a frequency-2 component can arise in one O(2) construction; it neither characterizes the full conditional basis nor proves completeness for O(2), much less arbitrary O(p,q). Moreover, the practical pooled condition can have zero vector components, so the assumed auxiliary multivector need not provide the direction required by Example 4.1.

The notion of completeness is not defined carefully for this nonlinear, input-dependent operator. A conditional kernel varying with f is not directly comparable to the basis of linear steerable kernels. The paper does not show that every conventional steerable kernel can be represented uniformly over inputs, or explain what completeness should mean when the conditioning statistic vanishes or changes.

The experiments do not test the claimed mechanism. There is no controlled kernel-fitting or harmonic-recovery experiment demonstrating reconstruction of the missing frequency-2 basis, and no ablation separating basis completion from the generic benefit of injecting a global summary. Comparisons such as CSCNN plus broadcast pooled features, alternative conditioning grades, scalar-only conditioning, and different pooling operators are absent.

The empirical evidence is insufficiently reported. Most principal results appear only as plots without numerical tables, uncertainty, numbers of runs, or statistical tests. Consequently, claims of significant and consistent superiority cannot be assessed. The SWE-5 results are mixed: the 55M model's 2.94% error is worse than CViT-B at 2.69%, CViT-L at 1.56%, and U-F2Net at 1.89%, despite the text suggesting performance on par with leading approaches.

The claimed practical efficiency is not substantiated by runtime, memory, or throughput measurements. Parameter matching alone does not establish comparable computational cost, especially because every sample generates its own convolution kernels. SWE-5 also uses unmatched model sizes and externally reported baseline numbers, weakening that comparison.

There is a theoretical-to-implementation gap concerning global pooling and exact E(p,q) equivariance. Mean pooling is not well-defined as a normalized operation over the infinite domain used in the theory, while the finite-grid circular mask described in Appendix B is centered and can break translation invariance. Finite-grid rotations also require discretization or interpolation. The single equivariance-error table does not specify transformations, angles, sample count, boundary handling, or variability, so it does not resolve these issues.

Some proofs and appendices need correction or strengthening. Appendix A.3 contains a tautological Eq. 33 rather than the intended equality, then invokes an “if and only if” conclusion that would require injectivity of the kernel network; only sufficiency is justified. Appendix A.4 describes a grade-1 relative-position vector but its code embeds both a scalar r and vector components, leaving the connection between the symbolic calculation and the stated argument unclear.

Reproducibility is poor. No code or artifact availability is stated, and essential training details such as learning rates, batch sizes, epoch or step counts, stopping criteria, random seeds, initialization, per-model hyperparameters, and exact baseline tuning are missing. The new relativistic Maxwell dataset is also under-specified, including its parameter distributions and precise outlier filtering. The anonymized hardware line is incomplete.

The paper acknowledges the unproved conjecture and the restrictive mean-field approximation, which is appropriate, but the title, abstract, and contribution statements still present completeness as an achieved result. Broader limitations—boundary-induced equivariance error, dependence on nonzero pooled features, compute costs, and lack of uncertainty estimates—are not discussed. No material research-ethics concern is apparent because the work uses physical simulations, but an explicit ethics or societal-impact statement is absent.

Overall, the equivariant conditional construction and preliminary PDE results have merit, but the headline theoretical result is not established and the evaluation is not sufficiently controlled or reproducible to support the paper's main explanatory and empirical claims. These are substantive issues requiring a reframed claim, stronger theory, and considerably more rigorous experiments.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete limitation of Clifford-Steerable CNNs: a single standard CSCNN layer cannot represent the frequency-2 component of the O(2) vector-to-vector kernel basis. The O(2) derivation and symbolic examples make this issue intuitive.

Conditioning the implicit kernel on equivariantly pooled input features is a simple, original, and potentially useful extension. The manuscript derives a conditional steerability constraint and gives a sufficient construction for retaining E(p,q)-equivariance.

The empirical scope is broad, covering Navier-Stokes, shallow-water, 3D Maxwell, and relativistic Maxwell problems. C-CSCNN consistently improves over the original CSCNN in the reported data-efficiency curves, often by substantial margins, and the measured equivariance error remains near numerical precision.

The method is presented clearly, relates well to prior work, and includes meaningful implementation and dataset information. Its use of global pooling adds little conceptual complexity and is applicable across Euclidean and pseudo-Euclidean settings.

The work has potentially significant practical value: it improves a general equivariant PDE architecture and produces competitive results even with a comparatively simple ResNet backbone. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: The central completeness claim is not established. Section 4.4 explicitly labels it a conjecture, and the analysis only shows that particular missing angular frequencies can arise in O(2) under suitable auxiliary multivectors. This neither proves completeness for O(2) nor for general O(p,q). Empirical forecasting accuracy cannot validate mathematical basis completeness, making the title and several claims substantially stronger than the evidence.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed explanation. There is no controlled ablation comparing global conditioning against other input-dependent kernels, invariant conditioning, or an analytically complete O(2) kernel basis. Thus, the improvements may come from sample-adaptive global context or added nonlinear capacity rather than recovery of the missing basis components.

Evaluation reporting is insufficiently rigorous for the strength of the empirical claims. Most results appear only as curves without complete numerical tables, variability, confidence intervals, numbers of random seeds, or statistical tests. Hyperparameter-selection fairness is also unclear because settings are inherited from different prior works and parameter matching is described only approximately.

Reproducibility is limited: the paper does not provide code or a release commitment, and omits important training details such as learning rates, batch sizes, training duration, warmup schedules, stopping criteria, and seeds. The newly generated relativistic Maxwell dataset also lacks a stated release mechanism and enough simulator parameters for straightforward reconstruction.

Efficiency claims are unsupported by timing or memory measurements. Although mean pooling is inexpensive, conditioning generates sample-dependent kernels and can reduce batching or kernel-reuse efficiency; the manuscript provides no throughput comparison. Likewise, the practical equivariance test lacks details about sampled transformations and discretization/interpolation effects.

The limitations discussion mentions mean-field conditioning and future alternatives, but does not squarely acknowledge the unresolved completeness claim, the absence of causal ablations, or the uncertainty in the reported comparisons. These are central rather than peripheral limitations. Overall, the idea and results are promising, but the unsupported headline claim and evidential gaps require substantial revision before the contribution can be relied upon.

strengths: Originality/significance: Conditioning an implicit Clifford-steerable kernel on an equivariant summary of the input is a simple, interesting extension of CSCNNs that could be useful beyond the evaluated PDEs.
Soundness: The manuscript derives an equivariance condition for conditional convolutions and reports very small single-layer numerical equivariance errors (3.4e-7 versus 2.4e-7 for CSCNN).

Empirical scope: Evaluation covers four PDE settings, including a pseudo-Euclidean spacetime task, several training-set sizes, and numerous baselines. C-CSCNN consistently and substantially improves over the original CSCNN, with negligible incremental inference cost (54.30 versus 53.83 ms).

Presentation: The motivation and construction are generally clear, and the paper openly discusses limitations such as discretization error, restricted field types, and the unresolved general O(p,q) case.

Ethics: The application domain presents no evident major ethical concern, and the impact statement appropriately discusses scientific and computational benefits without making high-risk deployment claims.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central completeness claim is not established. Example 4.6 and Appendix A.5 only exhibit particular angular terms, including a frequency-2 term, through symbolic calculations; they do not prove that the full O(2) kernel space is spanned, establish independence, or cover arbitrary input/output types. Section 4.4 calls completeness a conjecture and leaves its proof to future work, yet the abstract, conclusion, and limitations state that the paper shows or proves completeness for O(2,0). This is a material internal contradiction concerning the main theoretical claim.

Soundness: The practical equivariance claim does not cleanly follow from the theory. E(p,q)-equivariance requires the pooled condition to be translation invariant as well as O(p,q)-equivariant, but the implementation pools after applying a fixed, centered circular mask. Such masking is rotation compatible but generally changes under translations on a finite grid. The reported experiment tests only a single layer and provides insufficient details about sampled transformations; it therefore does not establish end-to-end E(p,q)-equivariance of the implemented models.

Evidence: The experiments do not isolate whether gains come from recovering the alleged missing kernel basis. A fixed random, non-equivariant condition improves SWE-1 MSE from 0.5699 to 0.3225, close to equivariant mean pooling at 0.2982. This suggests that much of the benefit may come from an additional symmetry-breaking reference or altered parameterization, but there is no comparison to complete analytical kernels, capacity-controlled alternatives, or direct kernel-basis measurements.

Evaluation/reproducibility: Results lack repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, and significance tests. Exact hyperparameters and baseline tuning procedures are largely deferred to prior papers, dataset construction and split descriptions are ambiguous (including statements about sampling from validation and test partitions), and no code or complete configuration artifact is provided. SWE-5 values are imported from prior work while model sizes differ substantially, weakening that comparison.

Significance: C-CSCNN convincingly improves its immediate CSCNN baseline, but it remains behind Transolver on both Maxwell tasks and behind several models on SWE-5. Thus the results support a useful specialized improvement more strongly than the broad state-of-the-art and expressivity claims.

Presentation: Important definitions and proofs are too informal for the stated generality. In particular, equivariance of the conditional kernel network is asserted largely by construction, and the step in Proposition 4.5 treating equality of kernel-network outputs as equivalent to equality of conditions implicitly requires an injectivity assumption that is neither stated nor generally true. These theoretical and reproducibility issues require substantial revision before others can reliably build on the contribution.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper identifies a concrete expressivity limitation of CSCNNs and proposes a simple input-conditioned kernel mechanism that adds negligible overhead relative to CSCNNs.

Soundness: The equivariance constraint for conditional convolution is a reasonable extension of steerable-convolution theory, and mean pooling is an appropriate equivariant conditioning operator in the idealized continuum setting.
Empirically, C-CSCNN consistently improves over the directly relevant CSCNN baseline across four PDE benchmarks, with especially substantial gains on Navier–Stokes and shallow-water forecasting.

Presentation is generally clear and visually polished, and the limitations and impact discussions appropriately acknowledge the unresolved general completeness question, discretization effects, and restricted field types.
The societal-risk discussion is adequate for this low-risk methodological work, with no evident unresolved ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim that conditioning restores a complete O(2) kernel basis is not established. Appendix A.5 only shows that some angular and frequency-2 terms can occur when additional multivectors are available; it does not show that every analytical steerable kernel can be represented, nor that the required terms remain available for arbitrary conditioning inputs. In particular, the pooled vector condition may be zero, and dependence on an input-derived orientation is not equivalent to recovering a fixed linear kernel basis.

The theoretical claim is internally inconsistent: Section 4.4 calls completeness a conjecture and explicitly leaves its proof to future work, whereas the conclusion and limitations state that completeness for O(2,0) was proved. The broader arbitrary-O(p,q) claim is supported neither theoretically nor by experiments capable of testing basis completeness.

The symbolic evidence is unreliable as presented. Code 1 describes a vector input but embeds it with a nonzero scalar component; Code 3 references an undefined y_clifford and prints kx[0] rather than the claimed two-product output k[0]. Thus the supplied snippets do not reproduce the stated argument.

Appendix A.3 contains an invalid “if and only if” step: equality of the kernel-network outputs does not imply equality of their inputs without injectivity. The proposition only needs a sufficient condition, but the written proof overclaims and even displays a tautological Eq. 37, reducing confidence in the formal development.

The finite-grid implementation does not justify the claimed E(p,q) equivariance. A centered circular mask is not translation invariant on a finite domain, arbitrary rotations do not preserve a Cartesian grid, and the equivariance experiment omits the sampled transformations, boundary handling, number of trials, and error variability.

The claim that max pooling preserves equivariance is generally false for componentwise pooling of vector or multivector coordinates under rotations. Moreover, the non-equivariant random condition performs nearly as well as mean pooling in Table 3, without repeated trials, so the ablation does not isolate the proposed equivariant mechanism.

Experimental evidence lacks multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, or statistical testing. Baseline training and tuning details are too sparse—models are merely said to be trained “to convergence,” with many hyperparameters omitted—and no code or generated MW2 dataset release is specified, substantially limiting reproducibility.

Several empirical conclusions are overstated. C-CSCNN remains behind Transolver on both Maxwell tasks, and the 55M-parameter SWE-5 model is worse than substantially smaller CViT-B and nearly twice the error of CViT-L. These results support improvement over CSCNN, but not a general state-of-the-art or “on par” claim. Overall, the empirical gains are promising, but they do not compensate for the unsupported central completeness claim and inadequate reproducibility.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper identifies a concrete expressivity limitation of Clifford-Steerable CNNs and proposes a simple, broadly applicable remedy—conditioning implicit kernels on equivariant summaries of the input. This is a useful conceptual extension of implicit steerable kernels.

Soundness: The derivation of the conditional-kernel steerability constraint is plausible, and the proposed mean-pooling construction gives a computationally efficient sufficient mechanism for preserving the intended symmetry in the idealized continuum setting.

Evaluation: Results cover four PDE settings and several symmetry signatures, including the relatively uncommon Lorentzian case. Parameter-matched comparisons show large, consistent gains over the original CSCNN, especially on Navier–Stokes and shallow-water tasks, while performance remains competitive with strong transformer and neural-operator baselines.

Efficiency: Mean conditioning adds only 0.87% inference overhead relative to CSCNN in the reported Maxwell experiment, so the empirical gains are not obtained by materially increasing the convolutional cost.

Presentation: The manuscript is well organized and generally clear, with helpful diagrams, explicit proofs, implementation discussion, ablations over conditioning operators, inference-time measurements, and an honest limitations section. The impact statement is appropriate and raises no material ethical concern. weaknesses: Soundness: The central completeness claim is not established. Section 4.4 labels completeness for arbitrary O(p,q) as Conjecture 4.7, while the O(2) argument only demonstrates that certain missing angular frequencies can be generated. It does not characterize the full conditional-kernel space or prove that all analytical steerable kernels are representable. The conclusion and limitations nevertheless state that completeness for O(2) was proved, creating a material overclaim.

The comparison with completeness of linear steerable kernels needs greater care because the proposed kernel depends on the input. Showing that a generic auxiliary multivector can generate frequency-2 terms does not show that every fixed linear steerable kernel can be recovered by an equivariant, input-dependent construction; for example, zero or symmetric pooled conditions can collapse back to the restricted case.

There is a continuum-to-implementation gap in the equivariance argument. Global mean pooling is translation invariant on an ideal full or periodic domain, but the implemented centered circular mask is generally not invariant to translations of the input. The paper measures a small E(2) error for one NS layer but does not specify sampled transformations or test the Lorentzian/noncompact setting, so the broad practical E(p,q)-equivariance claim is insufficiently validated.

Experimental uncertainty is not reported: there are no multiple-seed means, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Consequently, the robustness of model rankings—especially smaller gaps against Transolver or between pooling variants—is unclear.

Baseline fairness is only partially documented. Parameter matching is useful, but compute differs substantially: C-CSCNN takes 54.3 ms versus 39.1 ms for Transolver and 1.8 ms for a simple ResNet on MW3. SWE-5 baselines are imported from prior work with different parameter counts, and the tuning budget and training protocol equivalence are not established.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix gives architecture outlines, dataset sizes, hardware, and broad optimizer choices, but omits exact learning rates, batch sizes, schedules, training steps or stopping rules, random seeds, and code/release information. The newly generated relativistic Maxwell dataset also needs an accessible generation pipeline and fixed splits.

Presentation contains several claim inconsistencies and minor technical imprecision, including the conclusion saying completeness was theoretically shown and the limitations saying O(2) completeness was proved despite the main text presenting a conjectural argument. These should be corrected to distinguish demonstrated frequency recovery, formal equivariance, and conjectured general completeness.
